passages.text: Methane emissions from thermokarst lakes must emphasize the ice-melting impact on the Tibetan Plateau

Thermokarst lakes, serving as significant sources of methane (CH<sub>4</sub>), play a crucial role in affecting the feedback of permafrost carbon cycle to global warming. <sentence_start/>However, accurately assessing CH<sub>4</sub> emissions from these lakes remains challenging due to limited observations during lake ice melting periods. <sentence_start/>In this study, by integrating field surveys with machine learning modeling, we offer a comprehensive assessment of present and future CH<sub>4</sub> emissions from thermokarst lakes on the Tibetan Plateau. <sentence_start/>Our results reveal that the previously underestimated CH<sub>4</sub> release from lake ice bubble and water storage during ice melting periods is 11.2 ± 1.6 Gg C of CH<sub>4</sub>, accounting for 17 ± 4% of the annual total release from lakes. <sentence_start/>Despite thermokarst lakes cover only 0.2% of the permafrost area, they annually emit 65.5 ± 10.0 Gg C of CH<sub>4</sub>, which offsets 6.4% of the net carbon sink in alpine grasslands on the plateau. <sentence_start/>Considering the loss of lake ice, the expansion of thermokarst lakes is projected to lead to 1.1-1.2 folds increase in CH<sub>4</sub> emissions by 2100. <sentence_start/>Our study allows foreseeing future CH<sub>4</sub> emissions from the rapid expanding thermokarst lakes and sheds new lights on processes controlling the carbon-climate feedback in alpine permafrost ecosystems.
Methane emissions from thermokarst lakes on the Tibetan Plateau have likely been underestimated, according to the integration of field surveys with machine learning
Introduction

Permafrost regions, which cover approximately 22% of the Northern Hemisphere land area, store more than 50% of the world’s soil organic carbon<sup><citation ref-type="bibr" rid="CR1" doi="10.5194/bg-11-6573-2014" count="1">1</citation>,<citation ref-type="bibr" rid="CR2" doi="10.1038/s41467-018-08240-4" pmid="30651568" pmcid="PMC6335433" count="1">2</citation></sup>. <sentence_start/>The onset of global warming is triggering widespread abrupt permafrost thaw<citation ref-type="bibr" rid="CR3" doi="10.1038/s41561-019-0526-0" count="1"><sup>3</sup></citation>, which serves as a substantial source of land-atmosphere carbon exchange and has the potential to act as a positive feedback to climate warming<citation ref-type="bibr" rid="CR4" doi="10.1146/annurev-environ-012220-011847" count="1"><sup>4</sup></citation>. <sentence_start/>Thermokarst lakes, are characteristic features of abrupt permafrost thaw resulting from the melting of underground ice<citation ref-type="bibr" rid="CR5" doi="10.1038/ncomms13043" pmid="27725633" pmcid="PMC5062615" count="1"><sup>5</sup></citation>. <sentence_start/>These lakes play a crucial role in climate feedback due to their methane (CH<sub>4</sub>) emission potential compared to surrounding soils, yet they remain the most uncertain source of CH<sub>4</sub> emissions in the global permafrost zone<sup><citation ref-type="bibr" rid="CR6" doi="10.1029/2020GB006922" count="1">6</citation>-<citation ref-type="bibr" rid="CR8" doi="10.1016/j.earscirev.2020.103365" count="1">8</citation></sup>. <sentence_start/>Notably, large quantities of CH<sub>4</sub> are produced in the anaerobic environments of thermokarst lakes, becoming trapped in lake ice and the water body beneath the ice<sup><citation ref-type="bibr" rid="CR9" doi="10.1002/lol2.10079" count="1">9</citation>,<citation ref-type="bibr" rid="CR10" count="1">10</citation></sup>. <sentence_start/>Upon the melting of lake ice, CH<sub>4</sub> undergoes sudden release. <sentence_start/>However, due to the harsh alpine environment and high monitoring costs, in-situ measurements of lake CH<sub>4</sub> release, particularly during ice-covered and ice-melting periods are sparse, posing a significant challenge and hindering our understanding of CH<sub>4</sub> release dynamics from thermokarst lakes.

The Tibetan Plateau represents the largest alpine permafrost region globally, covering an area of 1.05 million km<sup>2</sup>, which accounts for roughly 75% of the total alpine permafrost regions in the Northern Hemisphere<sup><citation ref-type="bibr" rid="CR11" doi="10.5194/tc-11-2527-2017" count="1">11</citation>,<citation ref-type="bibr" rid="CR12" doi="10.1016/j.earscirev.2019.04.023" count="1">12</citation></sup>. <sentence_start/>This region stores an estimated 15.3-46.2 Pg of organic carbon in the top 3 meters of soil<citation ref-type="bibr" rid="CR13" doi="10.5194/essd-13-3453-2021" count="1"><sup>13</sup></citation>. <sentence_start/>Similar to the Arctic region, the Tibetan Plateau is experiencing rapid climate warming<citation ref-type="bibr" rid="CR14" count="1"><sup>14</sup></citation> and substantial permafrost thaw<citation ref-type="bibr" rid="CR2" doi="10.1038/s41467-018-08240-4" pmid="30651568" pmcid="PMC6335433" count="1"><sup>2</sup></citation>. <sentence_start/>Presently, it hosts over 160,000 thermokarst lakes, spanning approximately 2825 km<sup>2</sup> in total area<citation ref-type="bibr" rid="CR15" doi="10.1029/2021EA001950" count="1"><sup>15</sup></citation>. <sentence_start/>The expansion of these lakes is expanding across the plateau. <sentence_start/>Over the past three decades, the number and area of thermokarst lakes near the Qinghai-Tibet Highway have increased by 59% and 83%, respectively<citation ref-type="bibr" rid="CR16" count="1"><sup>16</sup></citation>. <sentence_start/>Changes in lake ice phenology, influencing the duration of ice cover, are undergoing significant alterations by modifying freeze-up and break-up times<citation ref-type="bibr" rid="CR17" count="1"><sup>17</sup></citation>. <sentence_start/>Thermokarst lakes emerge as important CH<sub>4</sub> sources on the Tibetan Plateau<sup><citation ref-type="bibr" rid="CR18" doi="10.1111/gcb.16658" pmid="36854541" count="1">18</citation>,<citation ref-type="bibr" rid="CR19" doi="10.1038/s41467-023-38907-6" pmid="37253726" pmcid="PMC10229571" count="1">19</citation></sup>. <sentence_start/>However, uncertainty persists regarding CH<sub>4</sub> emissions during ice-melting periods compared to the Arctic region, resulting in the underestimation of current CH<sub>4</sub> emissions on the Tibetan Plateau. <sentence_start/>Additionally, the absence of thermokarst lake simulations for CH<sub>4</sub> release in Earth system models stems from a poor understanding of CH<sub>4</sub> release dynamics, obscuring projections regarding future changes in CH<sub>4</sub> release from thermokarst lakes<sup><citation ref-type="bibr" rid="CR3" doi="10.1038/s41561-019-0526-0" count="1">3</citation>,<citation ref-type="bibr" rid="CR20" count="1">20</citation></sup>. <sentence_start/>These knowledge gaps impede the accurate prediction of carbon-climate feedback in alpine permafrost regions under forthcoming climate scenarios.

In this study, we conducted field observations of 56 thermokarst lakes during ice-covered periods (March-April) in 2023 and synthesized our previous measurements of CH<sub>4</sub> release from 162 thermokarst lakes during ice-free periods (May-October) on the Tibetan Plateau from 2019 to 2021<citation ref-type="bibr" rid="CR18" doi="10.1111/gcb.16658" pmid="36854541" count="1"><sup>18</sup></citation> (Fig. 1a, Supplementary Fig. 1, Supplementary Table 1). <sentence_start/>In this field survey, we collected the samples of lake ice and water beneath the ice by cutting a hole in the lake ice with a diameter of 30-50 cm (Fig. 1b-e). <sentence_start/>We measured dissolved CH<sub>4</sub> and CO<sub>2</sub> concentrations and their stable carbon isotopes to study CH<sub>4</sub> production pathways. <sentence_start/>Subsequently, we illustrated the patterns of CH<sub>4</sub> release during both ice-melting (including ice bubble and water storage) and ice-free periods (including ebullition and diffusion) on the whole plateau, thereby estimating the CH<sub>4</sub> emissions from thermokarst lakes. <sentence_start/>Finally, by integrating changes in the susceptibility distribution of thermokarst lake simulated by machine learning models, we predicted the expansion of thermokarst lakes and future changes in CH<sub>4</sub> emissions during the ice-melting and ice-free periods under Shared Socioeconomic Pathways (SSPs). <sentence_start/>We also separately presented future projections of CH<sub>4</sub> emissions from thermokarst lakes with and without considering the loss of lake ice.<sentence_start/>Fig. 1

Results and Discussion
CH<sub>4</sub> emission pathways

To explore the difference in dissolved CH<sub>4</sub> concentrations between ice-free and ice-covered periods on the Tibetan Plateau, we conducted field observations in March-April 2023 and integrated our published data from thermokarst lakes during 2019-2023<citation ref-type="bibr" rid="CR18" doi="10.1111/gcb.16658" pmid="36854541" count="1"><sup>18</sup></citation>. <sentence_start/>The same sampling method was used in two periods in order to narrow the uncertainty (See Methods). <sentence_start/>Results indicate that during ice-covered period, the median concentration of dissolved CH<sub>4</sub> in the water body beneath lake ice is 2.61 μmol/L (<italic>n</italic> = 151; Fig. 1f), with a wide range from 0.03-280.47 μmol/L. <sentence_start/>Conversely, during ice-free period, the median dissolved CH<sub>4</sub> concentration in lake water is 0.88 μmol/L, ranging from 0.01-39.98 μmol/L (<italic>n</italic> = 353; Fig. 1f). <sentence_start/>Dissolved CH<sub>4</sub> concentrations during ice-covered period significantly surpass those in the ice-free period (<italic>p</italic> < 0.001), with concentrations within the same thermokarst lake reaching up to 100 times higher in the ice-covered period. <sentence_start/>It is attributable to that methanogenesis continues under the lake ice due to the anaerobic environment and the barrier effect of lake ice<sup><citation ref-type="bibr" rid="CR9" doi="10.1002/lol2.10079" count="1">9</citation>,<citation ref-type="bibr" rid="CR21" doi="10.1029/2019JG005078" count="1">21</citation></sup>, leading to the accumulation and entrapment of CH<sub>4</sub> in ice-covered thermokarst lakes. <sentence_start/>Interestingly, dissolved CH<sub>4</sub> concentrations during ice-covered and ice-free periods exhibit significantly positive correlations (Fig. 1g, Supplementary Table 2).

Additionally, dissolved CH<sub>4</sub> concentrations are closely related to sediment organic carbon content in thermokarst lakes with different vegetation types on the Tibetan Plateau (Supplementary Fig. 2). <sentence_start/>This is attributable to that methanogenesis primarily occurs in the lake sediments, where organic carbon provides crucial substrate for microbial CH<sub>4</sub> production<sup><citation ref-type="bibr" rid="CR22" doi="10.1016/j.scitotenv.2021.149692" pmid="34428650" count="1">22</citation>-<citation ref-type="bibr" rid="CR24" doi="10.4319/lo.2009.54.6_part_2.2298" count="1">24</citation></sup>. <sentence_start/>The gradient of sediment organic carbon contents in thermokarst lakes is controlled by soil organic carbon around the lakes within the watersheds, which is transported into the thermokarst lakes through hydrological processes<sup><citation ref-type="bibr" rid="CR25" doi="10.1016/j.scitotenv.2022.154761" pmid="35339557" count="1">25</citation>,<citation ref-type="bibr" rid="CR26" doi="10.1007/s10533-022-00914-y" count="1">26</citation></sup>. <sentence_start/>Thus, the highest CH<sub>4</sub> concentrations are found in thermokarst lakes under the vegetation of alpine swamp meadows (ASM) and meadows (AM), followed by alpine steppe (AS) and desert (AD), evident both ice-covered and ice-free periods (Supplementary Fig. 3). <sentence_start/>It was shown that sediment organic carbon contents in the thermokarst lakes is closely related to vegetation types on the Tibetan Plateau<sup><citation ref-type="bibr" rid="CR18" doi="10.1111/gcb.16658" pmid="36854541" count="1">18</citation>,<citation ref-type="bibr" rid="CR25" doi="10.1016/j.scitotenv.2022.154761" pmid="35339557" count="1">25</citation></sup>. <sentence_start/>The results suggest that large amounts of CH<sub>4</sub> are trapped in ice-covered thermokarst lakes, exhibiting similar patterns to those during ice-free period.

Furthermore, to elucidate the pathways of CH<sub>4</sub> production in thermokarst lakes during ice-covered periods on the Tibetan Plateau, we calculated the carbon fractionation factor (α<sub>C</sub>) using δ<sup>13</sup>C values of dissolved CO<sub>2</sub> and CH<sub>4.</sub> <sentence_start/>The α<sub>C</sub> values greater than 1.055 indicate CH<sub>4</sub> origin predominantly via CO<sub>2</sub> reduction, while values between 1.040 and 1.055 suggest acetate fermentation<sup><citation ref-type="bibr" rid="CR27" count="1">27</citation>,<citation ref-type="bibr" rid="CR28" doi="10.1016/S0009-2541(99)00092-3" count="1">28</citation></sup>. <sentence_start/>The α<sub>C</sub> values below 1.040 are likely associated with CH<sub>4</sub> oxidation<citation ref-type="bibr" rid="CR29" doi="10.1016/j.geoderma.2009.08.023" count="1"><sup>29</sup></citation> (see Methods). <sentence_start/>Results show that the observed δ<sup>13</sup>C-CH<sub>4</sub> in the water body beneath lake ice has a median value of −57.9‰ (ranging from −89.6‰ - −26.7‰) (Supplementary Fig. 4a), similar to that of diffusion during ice-free periods on the Tibetan Plateau. <sentence_start/>The median α<sub>C</sub> value of water storage during ice-covered periods is 1.038 (<italic>n</italic> = 140) (Supplementary Fig. 4b), which indicates that acetate fermentation is the primary pathway for CH<sub>4</sub> production during ice-covered periods, accompanied by significant oxidation<sup><citation ref-type="bibr" rid="CR27" count="1">27</citation>,<citation ref-type="bibr" rid="CR29" doi="10.1016/j.geoderma.2009.08.023" count="1">29</citation>-<citation ref-type="bibr" rid="CR31" count="1">31</citation></sup>. <sentence_start/>This finding further implies that CH<sub>4</sub> production continues throughout the winter in the Tibetan Plateau thermokarst lakes. <sentence_start/>Meanwhile, this pathway aligns with that of CH<sub>4</sub> emissions via diffusion during ice-free periods<citation ref-type="bibr" rid="CR18" doi="10.1111/gcb.16658" pmid="36854541" count="1"><sup>18</sup></citation>, but contrasts with that via ebullition during ice-free periods, which is predominantly driven by CO<sub>2</sub> reduction on the Tibetan Plateau<citation ref-type="bibr" rid="CR19" doi="10.1038/s41467-023-38907-6" pmid="37253726" pmcid="PMC10229571" count="1"><sup>19</sup></citation>. <sentence_start/>Similarly, high-emission point sources and hotspots in Siberian lakes are primarily driven by CO<sub>2</sub> reduction, while lower-emission processes are influenced by acetate fermentation<citation ref-type="bibr" rid="CR27" count="1"><sup>27</sup></citation>. <sentence_start/>However, in Western Greenland, it was shown that the primary production pathway for CH<sub>4</sub> released through ebullition is acetate fermentation<citation ref-type="bibr" rid="CR32" doi="10.1007/s10533-016-0261-1" count="1"><sup>32</sup></citation>, whereas in Finland, CH₄ emissions via diffusion are mainly driven by CO<sub>2</sub> reduction<citation ref-type="bibr" rid="CR33" doi="10.1007/s00027-015-0410-y" count="1"><sup>33</sup></citation>. <sentence_start/>The discrepancy is attributed to that the different composition of microbial communities in aquatic systems can control the CH<sub>4</sub> production pathways<sup><citation ref-type="bibr" rid="CR34" doi="10.3390/biology13080615" pmcid="PMC11351834" pmid="39194553" count="1">34</citation>,<citation ref-type="bibr" rid="CR35" doi="10.1134/S0026261721020065" count="1">35</citation></sup>. <sentence_start/>Additionally, the environmental factors, such as temperature<citation ref-type="bibr" rid="CR36" doi="10.1016/j.envint.2021.106575" pmid="33901975" count="1"><sup>36</sup></citation>, salinity<citation ref-type="bibr" rid="CR19" doi="10.1038/s41467-023-38907-6" pmid="37253726" pmcid="PMC10229571" count="1"><sup>19</sup></citation>, and substrates available for methanogenesis<citation ref-type="bibr" rid="CR37" doi="10.1111/gcb.16151" pmcid="PMC9310722" pmid="35243729" count="1"><sup>37</sup></citation>, can further influence the pathway of CH<sub>4</sub> production.

Under future climate scenarios, shorter ice-covered periods and warmer lake water are expected to enhance the proportion of CH<sub>4</sub> ebullitive emissions from thermokarst lakes on the Tibetan Plateau. <sentence_start/>Particularly, changes in lake water temperature and dissolved oxygen content can shift the methanogenic pathway, with more CH<sub>4</sub> likely released through ebullition driven by CO<sub>2</sub> reduction<citation ref-type="bibr" rid="CR36" doi="10.1016/j.envint.2021.106575" pmid="33901975" count="1"><sup>36</sup></citation>, potentially increasing future total CH<sub>4</sub> emissions from thermokarst lakes. <sentence_start/>Although regional divergence exists in the CH<sub>4</sub> accumulation during ice-covered periods<sup><citation ref-type="bibr" rid="CR38" doi="10.1029/2024GB008106" count="1">38</citation>-<citation ref-type="bibr" rid="CR40" doi="10.5194/tc-15-1607-2021" count="1">40</citation></sup>, potentially affecting future CH<sub>4</sub> emission prediction, the results shed light on the mechanistic understanding of CH<sub>4</sub> release dynamics in the Tibetan Plateau thermokarst lakes. <sentence_start/>Our study highlights the need to account for winter CH<sub>4</sub> production in thermokarst lakes, which may substantially contribute to future annual CH<sub>4</sub> emissions under ongoing climate warming.
CH<sub>4</sub> flux in ice-melting and ice-free periods

To systematically evaluate the total annual CH<sub>4</sub> release from thermokarst lakes on the Tibetan Plateau, we quantified the water storage and ice bubble storage by conducting the field observations during ice-cover periods and synthesizing our published fluxes during ice-free period<citation ref-type="bibr" rid="CR18" doi="10.1111/gcb.16658" pmid="36854541" count="1"><sup>18</sup></citation> (see Methods). <sentence_start/>During ice-melting periods, we calculated the proportions of CH<sub>4</sub> flux between ice bubble and water storage with different vegetation types (Supplementary Fig. 5). <sentence_start/>The result shows that during the ice-melting period, CH<sub>4</sub> release from thermokarst lakes primarily originates from water storage (Fig. 2a). <sentence_start/>The median CH<sub>4</sub> release flux from water storage is 0.8 (0.01-39.9) g m<sup>−2</sup> yr<sup>−1</sup>, while CH<sub>4</sub> release from ice bubble occurs at a rate of 0.3 (0-17.0) g m<sup>−2</sup> yr<sup>−1</sup> (Fig. 2a), corroborating recent observations<citation ref-type="bibr" rid="CR38" doi="10.1029/2024GB008106" count="1"><sup>38</sup></citation>. <sentence_start/>Combined, the total CH<sub>4</sub> release from ice bubble and water storage ranges from 0.01-56.9 g m<sup>−2</sup> yr<sup>−1</sup>, with a median of 1.1 g m<sup>−2</sup> yr<sup>−1</sup>. <sentence_start/>Similarly, we observed a distribution pattern of CH<sub>4</sub> release flux from thermokarst lakes under different vegetation type within the watershed (Fig. 2b). <sentence_start/>Our study reveals that water storage and ice bubble are estimated to contribute 71.1% and 28.9% to the CH<sub>4</sub> release from thermokarst lakes during the ice-melting periods, respectively.<sentence_start/>Fig. 2

To estimate the proportions of ebullition and diffusion release for annual CH<sub>4</sub> emissions, we collected and analyzed the previous data of CH<sub>4</sub> emissions during ice-free period<citation ref-type="bibr" rid="CR19" doi="10.1038/s41467-023-38907-6" pmid="37253726" pmcid="PMC10229571" count="1"><sup>19</sup></citation> (Supplementary Fig. 6). <sentence_start/>Our results show that the median CH<sub>4</sub> release flux is 13.6 (0.1-481.4) g m<sup>−2</sup> yr<sup>−1</sup>, with 2.0 (0.01-71.5) g m<sup>−2</sup> yr<sup>−1</sup> for diffusion and 11.2 (0.1-422.6) g m<sup>−2</sup> yr<sup>−1</sup> for ebullition (Fig. 2c). <sentence_start/>The highest CH<sub>4</sub> fluxes are also found in thermokarst lakes under vegetation type of ASM with a median of 30.7 g m<sup>−2</sup> yr<sup>−1</sup>, followed by AM, AS and AD (Fig. 2d). <sentence_start/>The proportions of CH<sub>4</sub> release from thermokarst lakes through diffusion and ebullition are 15.6% and 84.4%, respectively. <sentence_start/>By comparing CH<sub>4</sub> release flux between the ice-melting and ice-free period, we show that the contribution of CH<sub>4</sub> release during ice-melting is essential for the annual estimation, accounting for 5.2-25.8% of the total release from these lakes (Fig. 2e). <sentence_start/>Although lower water temperatures and reduced external hydrological inputs typically limit the CH<sub>4</sub> production, microbial activity continues in both the water column and sediments, even when fully covered by ice<sup><citation ref-type="bibr" rid="CR9" doi="10.1002/lol2.10079" count="1">9</citation>,<citation ref-type="bibr" rid="CR41" doi="10.4319/lo.2013.58.6.1998" count="1">41</citation></sup>. <sentence_start/>Additionally, significant inputs of allochthonous organic matter during the early and late ice-covered periods<citation ref-type="bibr" rid="CR42" doi="10.1002/lno.10549" count="1"><sup>42</sup></citation>, promote the decomposition of organic matter, leading to a high proportion of CH<sub>4</sub> emissions during the ice-melting period. <sentence_start/>Notably, the lake ice covered period account for approximately 40% for a year on the Tibetan Plateau<citation ref-type="bibr" rid="CR43" doi="10.3390/rs10101534" count="1"><sup>43</sup></citation>.
Annual emissions

To estimate the extent of previously underestimated CH<sub>4</sub> release on the Tibetan Plateau, we used a Monte Carlo approach to randomly sample thermokarst lake CH<sub>4</sub> flux for each vegetation type. <sentence_start/>We then obtained the total annual CH<sub>4</sub> emissions by multiplying the area of thermokarst lakes and mean CH<sub>4</sub> flux under each vegetation type. <sentence_start/>Results indicate that during ice-free period, thermokarst lakes emit CH<sub>4</sub> at a rate of 54.2 ± 9.9 Gg C yr<sup>−1</sup>, with 46.9 ± 9.8 Gg C yr<sup>−1</sup> from ebullition and 7.3 ± 1.4 Gg C yr<sup>−1</sup> from diffusion. <sentence_start/>During ice-melting period, CH<sub>4</sub> emission is estimated at 11.2 ± 1.6 Gg C yr<sup>−1</sup>, with 3.3 ± 0.6 Gg C yr<sup>−1</sup> released from bubbles trapped within lake ice, and 7.9 ± 1.5 Gg C yr<sup>−1</sup> from the water body beneath lake ice. <sentence_start/>The total annual CH<sub>4</sub> emissions from thermokarst lakes on the Tibetan Plateau are estimated to be 65.5 ± 10.0 Gg C yr<sup>−1</sup>. <sentence_start/>Our study reveals that previously overlooked CH<sub>4</sub> emissions during ice-melting period account for 17.1% (13.5-20.7%) of the annual CH<sub>4</sub> emissions, with 5.0% (3.8-6.2%) attributed to ice bubbles and 12.1% (9.2-15.0%) from water storage (Table 1, Supplementary Fig. 7a). <sentence_start/>The contributions of CH<sub>4</sub> emissions during ice-melting period to the whole year vary with vegetation types of alpine swamp meadow (25.8%), alpine meadow (16.9%), alpine steppe (11.5%) and alpine desert (5.2%) (Fig. 2e, Supplementary Fig. 7b). <sentence_start/>Compared with the Arctic region, where the contribution of CH<sub>4</sub> release during ice-melting was 20-74%<sup><citation ref-type="bibr" rid="CR7" doi="10.1038/ngeo2578" count="1">7</citation>,<citation ref-type="bibr" rid="CR44" doi="10.1016/s0045-6535(02)00148-0" pmid="12653296" Expansion of thermokarst lake

To predict future changes of thermokarst lakes on the Tibetan Plateau, we used the Random Forest (RF) model to assess the susceptibility distribution of thermokarst lakes and calculate the actual area of thermokarst lake based on the lake area density under different vegetation types (Supplementary Table 5) (see Methods). <sentence_start/>The results show that thermokarst lakes on the Tibetan Plateau are expected to increase under SSP scenarios. <sentence_start/>By 2100, the total area of thermokarst lakes is projected to reach 3912 km<sup>2</sup> (increase by 85.9% compared with 2020) under SSP1-2.6, 3926 km<sup>2</sup> (86.5%) under SSP2-4.5, and 4102 km<sup>2</sup> (94.9%) under SSP5-8.5 (Supplementary Fig. 8). <sentence_start/>These changes correspond with the previous remote sensing observations that showing an increase of 14.7% per-decade between 1969 and 2010 and 20.0% per-decade between 2010 and 2019<citation ref-type="bibr" rid="CR51" doi="10.1016/j.catena.2022.106497" count="1"><sup>51</sup></citation>. <sentence_start/>Our results forecast thermokarst lakes area will increase by 33.2% per decade between 2020-2040, which is higher than the previous increasing rate due to future warming and wetting in the alpine region (Supplementary Fig. 9). <sentence_start/>Although future prediction of thermokarst lakes relies more on the process model and need more verification, abrupt permafrost thaw cannot be simulated by Earth System Models (ESMs). <sentence_start/>Our results show the response of these lakes on the Tibetan Plateau to future climate change through considering the influencing factors of climate, topography, hydrology, soil, permafrost, and human activity (Supplementary Table 3). <sentence_start/>Our study highlights the future changes of alpine thermokarst lakes and their ecological and environmental impacts.

Our study offers advantages in simulating CH<sub>4</sub> emissions from thermokarst lakes. <sentence_start/>Firstly, by integrating the distribution of thermokarst lakes and environmental factors, we predicted the future changes in thermokarst lake area on the Tibetan Plateau. <sentence_start/>Secondly, although our simulations do not include dynamic vegetation changes expected in Tibetan Plateau permafrost regions with warming, we consider the effects of vegetation and climate on the current distribution of thermokarst lakes in order to reduce the uncertainty in estimating CH<sub>4</sub> emissions. <sentence_start/>Furthermore, given that thermokarst lakes affect small areas within the permafrost region, changes in vegetation may not be the primary determinant of CH<sub>4</sub> emissions compared to widespread gradual permafrost thaw emissions<citation ref-type="bibr" rid="CR3" doi="10.1038/s41561-019-0526-0" count="1"><sup>3</sup></citation>. <sentence_start/>Finally, by integrating field observations of CH<sub>4</sub> release, analysis of dissolved δ<sup>13</sup>C-CH<sub>4</sub> and CO<sub>2</sub>, and future predictions, we provide current and future changes in previously underestimated CH<sub>4</sub> release during ice-melting from thermokarst lakes (Fig. 4). <sentence_start/>Our study also identifies additional important knowledge gaps, such as the verification of lake expansion and spatial heterogeneity of lake ice phenology, that will require further research before carbon release from thermokarst lakes can be simulated by ESMs.<sentence_start/>Fig. 4

Implications

The exploration into the dynamics of thermokarst lakes and their impact on climate change yields invaluable insights with far-reaching implications for both scientific understanding and proactive mitigation strategies. <sentence_start/>This study delves into the significance of these research findings and outlines potential strategies to address the challenges posed by thermokarst lake dynamics in the context of climate change. <sentence_start/>First and foremost, the research on thermokarst lakes underscores their pivotal role in the carbon cycle and climate feedback loop. <sentence_start/>By quantifying previously underestimated CH<sub>4</sub> emissions, particularly during ice-melting periods, studies have illuminated a critical aspect of permafrost thaw dynamics. <sentence_start/>This enhanced understanding not only refines our knowledge of regional carbon dynamics but also highlights the urgency of addressing these emissions to mitigate climate change.

One of the key values of this research lies in its contribution to improving ESMs and climate projections. <sentence_start/>By integrating field observations, machine learning modeling, and projections from climate models, researchers have laid the groundwork for more accurate simulations of thermokarst lake dynamics and their implications for future climate scenarios. <sentence_start/>This advancement is instrumental in informing climate policy decisions and developing adaptive strategies to mitigate the impacts of permafrost thaw. <sentence_start/>Furthermore, the insights gleaned from thermokarst lake research offer valuable guidance for policymakers and stakeholders seeking to address the challenges posed by climate change. <sentence_start/>From enhancing monitoring efforts to implementing targeted mitigation measures, there are several avenues for action. <sentence_start/>Investing in enhanced monitoring permafrost thaw and remote sensing techniques is essential to capture the spatial variability of thermokarst lakes and track their evolution over time<sup><citation ref-type="bibr" rid="CR60" doi="10.3390/rs15184396" count="1">60</citation>,<citation ref-type="bibr" rid="CR61" doi="10.3390/rs15133331" count="1">61</citation></sup>. <sentence_start/>This comprehensive data collection is crucial for refining climate models and improving the accuracy of future projections.

Moreover, proactive mitigation strategies are imperative to mitigate the impacts of thermokarst lake dynamics on the climate system<citation ref-type="bibr" rid="CR62" doi="10.1007/s40641-017-0054-1" count="1"><sup>62</sup></citation>. <sentence_start/>This includes measures to reduce anthropogenic greenhouse gas emissions<citation ref-type="bibr" rid="CR63" doi="10.1029/2019RG000675" count="1"><sup>63</sup></citation>, as well as targeted interventions to mitigate CH<sub>4</sub> emissions from thermokarst lakes<citation ref-type="bibr" rid="CR64" doi="10.1021/es204686w" pmid="22594483" count="1"><sup>64</sup></citation>. <sentence_start/>Strategies such as lake management techniques, habitat restoration, and land-use planning can help minimize the release of CH<sub>4</sub> and mitigate the climate feedback effects of thermokarst lakes. <sentence_start/>Research on thermokarst lakes offers invaluable insights into the complex dynamics of permafrost thaw and its implications for global climate change. <sentence_start/>By enhancing our understanding of CH<sub>4</sub> emissions from thermokarst lakes and refining climate models, this research provides a foundation for informed decision-making and proactive climate mitigation strategies. <sentence_start/>Moving forward, continued investment in research, monitoring, and mitigation efforts is essential to address the challenges posed by thermokarst lakes and safeguard the stability of the global climate system.
Methods
Study area and field observations

Permafrost is widely distributed across the Tibetan Plateau, covering approximately 50% of the Plateau<citation ref-type="bibr" rid="CR12" doi="10.1016/j.earscirev.2019.04.023" count="1"><sup>12</sup></citation>. <sentence_start/>The annual mean ground temperature has increased by 0.43 °C per decade<citation ref-type="bibr" rid="CR65" count="1"><sup>65</sup></citation>, resulting in a significant deepening of the active layer<sup><citation ref-type="bibr" rid="CR66" doi="10.1016/j.earscirev.2020.103433" count="1">66</citation>-<citation ref-type="bibr" rid="CR68" doi="10.1016/j.geoderma.2021.115083" count="1">68</citation></sup>. <sentence_start/>Thermokarst lakes are widely distributed on the permafrost regions and are dominated by lakes with small surface areas (<10,000 m<sup>2</sup>), which account for ~80% of the total. <sentence_start/>In this study, we measured the dissolved CH<sub>4</sub> concentrations in 56 alpine thermokarst lakes during ice-covered period in 2023. <sentence_start/>Furthermore, we integrated CH<sub>4</sub> concentrations data from 162 thermokarst lakes during ice-free period on the Tibetan Plateau (Fig. 1a)<citation ref-type="bibr" rid="CR18" doi="10.1111/gcb.16658" pmid="36854541" count="1"><sup>18</sup></citation>, all located within the same study area. <sentence_start/>The observed lakes are primarily located in the continuous permafrost regions with elevations between 4210 and 5127 m (Fig. 1a). <sentence_start/>The area of thermokarst lakes ranges from 373 m<sup>2</sup> to 648,966 m<sup>2</sup>, with the majority being less than 100,000 m<sup>2</sup> (Supplementary Fig. 1b, Supplementary Table. 1).

Based on the dataset of vegetation type distribution on the Tibetan Plateau<citation ref-type="bibr" rid="CR69" doi="10.1007/s11629-015-3485-y" count="1"><sup>69</sup></citation>, the observed thermokarst lakes are mainly distributed in the regions with four vegetation types: alpine swamp meadow (ASM), alpine meadow (AM), alpine steppe (AS) and alpine desert (AD). <sentence_start/>These regions exhibit distinct differences in vegetation composition, soil characteristics, and organic carbon content. <sentence_start/>ASM is characterized by sedges and rushes, with saturated soils rich in organic matter and high moisture levels, which supports significant carbon sequestration<sup><citation ref-type="bibr" rid="CR70" doi="10.5194/bg-19-861-2022" count="1">70</citation>,<citation ref-type="bibr" rid="CR71" doi="10.3390/rs13040669" count="1">71</citation></sup>. <sentence_start/>AM features grasses and herbs, with well-drained loamy soils and moderate organic carbon content, experiencing seasonal freeze-thaw cycles<citation ref-type="bibr" rid="CR71" doi="10.3390/rs13040669" count="1"><sup>71</sup></citation>. <sentence_start/>AS comprises drought-tolerant grasses and shrubs, with dry, coarse soils and low organic carbon content, showing significant spatial variability<citation ref-type="bibr" rid="CR71" doi="10.3390/rs13040669" count="1"><sup>71</sup></citation>. <sentence_start/>AD is characterized by sparse vegetation, very dry rocky soils, and minimal organic carbon, with high pH levels and significant wind erosion<citation ref-type="bibr" rid="CR72" doi="10.3389/fmicb.2022.1007194" pmid="36578569" pmcid="PMC9791195" count="1"><sup>72</sup></citation>. <sentence_start/>During ice-covered period from March to April 2023, the dissolved CH<sub>4</sub> in lake water was collected using the headspace equilibrium method (Fig. 1e)<sup><citation ref-type="bibr" rid="CR73" doi="10.1002/lno.10298" count="1">73</citation>,<citation ref-type="bibr" rid="CR74" doi="10.1126/science.251.4991.298" pmid="17733287" count="1">74</citation></sup>. <sentence_start/>In each lake, 3-6 sampling points were distributed from the edge to the center of lake. <sentence_start/>Briefly, 400 mL of surface water from a depth of 15 cm was collected with a 500 mL syringe after removing surface ice with a chainsaw (Fig. 1b), Subsequently, 100 mL of pure N<sub>2</sub> was injected into the syringe, and the syringe was immediately shaken for 3 minutes to equilibrate the headspace in the field. <sentence_start/>A 100 mL of the headspace gas was transferred from the syringe into a specialized aluminum foil gas sampling bag, which was then sealed for preservation. <sentence_start/>At each sampling point, two gas samples were collected for At each sampling point, we also measured water quality parameters, including water temperature, dissolved oxygen and conductivity, using a multi-parameter water quality meter (Fig. 1d). <sentence_start/>Meteorological data, including air temperature, atmospheric pressure, and wind speed, were sourced from automated field weather stations located at Liangdao River, Tanggula, and Beilu River, as well as from the National Meteorological Science Data Center (NMSDC; ) for the Maduo, Wudao Liang, and Tuotuo River.

The ice cover on thermokarst lakes acts as a barrier during frozen periods, preventing CH<sub>4</sub> release into the atmosphere. <sentence_start/>As the lake ice melts during the spring season, the accumulated CH<sub>4</sub> is released at a higher flux<citation ref-type="bibr" rid="CR86" doi="10.1038/ngeo2795" count="1"><sup>86</sup></citation>. <sentence_start/>The sealed CH<sub>4</sub> can be divided into two segments during ice-covered period: water storage and ice bubble storage<sup><citation ref-type="bibr" rid="CR7" doi="10.1038/ngeo2578" count="1">7</citation>,<citation ref-type="bibr" rid="CR10" count="1">10</citation>,<citation ref-type="bibr" rid="CR81" doi="10.1111/j.1600-0889.2007.00301.x" count="1">81</citation>,<citation ref-type="bibr" rid="CR87" doi="10.5194/bg-11-6791-2014" count="1">87</citation>,<citation ref-type="bibr" rid="CR88" doi="10.5194/bg-12-3197-2015" count="1">88</citation></sup>. <sentence_start/>Water storage refers to dissolved CH<sub>4</sub> in water, remaining confined within the lake water until the ice breaks. <sentence_start/>During this process, a portion of the CH<sub>4</sub> undergoes oxidization, with roughly half of it being transformed<citation ref-type="bibr" rid="CR87" doi="10.5194/bg-11-6791-2014" count="1"><sup>87</sup></citation>. <sentence_start/>During ice-melting period, CH<sub>4</sub> is released into the atmosphere through diffusion. <sentence_start/>Throughout these periods, as the CH<sub>4</sub> concentration in the lake water steadily decreases, the diffusion flux correspondingly diminishes as well. <sentence_start/>When calculating the CH<sub>4</sub> flux, we consider the 14 days before and after ice-free period as the high and low emission periods<citation ref-type="bibr" rid="CR76" doi="10.1016/j.catena.2023.107454" count="1"><sup>76</sup></citation>. <sentence_start/>CH<sub>4</sub> flux from water storage were calculated using Eqs. Pathway of CH<sub>4</sub> production

To evaluate the pathway of CH<sub>4</sub> production, we measured the δ<sup>13</sup>C isotope abundance of both CO<sub>2</sub> and CH<sub>4</sub> and calculated the apparent fractionation factor (α<sub>C</sub>). <sentence_start/>Stable carbon isotope analysis of CO<sub>2</sub> and CH<sub>4</sub> was conducted using an isotopic ratio mass spectrometry. <sentence_start/>The α<sub>C</sub> was calculated from δ<sup>13</sup>C of CH<sub>4</sub> and CO<sub>2</sub> using Eq. (20)<citation ref-type="bibr" rid="CR18" doi="10.1111/gcb.16658" pmid="36854541" count="1"><sup>18</sup></citation>. <sentence_start/>The δ<sup>13</sup>C isotope abundance of CO<sub>2</sub> and CH<sub>4</sub> released from diffusion and ebullition during ice-free period were analyzed from published data<sup><citation ref-type="bibr" rid="CR18" doi="10.1111/gcb.16658" pmid="36854541" count="1">18</citation>,<citation ref-type="bibr" rid="CR19" doi="10.1038/s41467-023-38907-6" pmid="37253726" pmcid="PMC10229571" count="1">19</citation></sup>. <sentence_start/>If α<sub>C</sub> is between 1.040 and 1.055, it suggests that CH<sub>4</sub> production in thermokarst lakes is mainly through acetate fermentation (AM); and α<sub>C</sub> is greater than 1.055, it indicates that CH<sub>4</sub> production is primarily driven by CO₂ reduction<sup><citation ref-type="bibr" rid="CR27" count="1">27</citation>,<citation ref-type="bibr" rid="CR28" doi="10.1016/S0009-2541(99)00092-3" count="1">28</citation></sup>. <sentence_start/>When α<sub>C</sub> is less than 1.040, it indicates that CH<sub>4</sub> oxidation is the dominant process in thermokarst lakes<citation ref-type="bibr" rid="CR29" doi="10.1016/j.geoderma.2009.08.023" count="1"><sup>29</sup></citation>.
Regional upscaling

Based on 409 CH<sub>4</sub> fluxes data during ice-free and ice-melting period, this study uses Monte Carlo analysis to estimate the annual CH<sub>4</sub> emissions and their uncertainties from thermokarst lakes on the Tibetan Plateau. <sentence_start/>For each vegetation type (including alpine swamp meadow, alpine meadow, alpine steppe, and alpine desert)<citation ref-type="bibr" rid="CR69" doi="10.1007/s11629-015-3485-y" count="1"><sup>69</sup></citation>, 1000 iterations were performed for both the ice-melting period and ice-free period. <sentence_start/>In each iteration, a random value was sampled from the thermokarst lake CH<sub>4</sub> flux data and multiplied by the total area of thermokarst lakes for each vegetation type<citation ref-type="bibr" rid="CR15" doi="10.1029/2021EA001950" count="1"><sup>15</sup></citation>. <sentence_start/>Finally, the annual CH<sub>4</sub> emissions from thermokarst lakes under different vegetation type were calculated to determine total CH<sub>4</sub> emissions. <sentence_start/>We used the mean value of the results from the Monte Carlo analysis as the total CH<sub>4</sub> emissions from thermokarst lakes on the Tibetan Plateau.
Thermokarst lake susceptibility

We analyzed a total of 161,341 thermokarst lakes<citation ref-type="bibr" rid="CR15" doi="10.1029/2021EA001950" count="1"><sup>15</sup></citation>. <sentence_start/>Prior to machine learning modeling, we used the ENMTools to filter out redundant samples, ensuring that only one lake was present in each 0.0083° × 0.0083° grid. <sentence_start/>Ultimately, we selected 71164 thermokarst lakes as training samples for the model. <sentence_start/>Meanwhile, we selected nine environmental factors influencing the distribution of thermokarst lakes. <sentence_start/>These factors include topography, hydrology, soil, human activities, permafrost and climate (Supplementary Table 3). <sentence_start/>The topographic factors, including elevation and slope, was derived from the high-precision Global Digital Elevation Model (DEM) (ETOPO Global Relief Model, National Centers for Environmental Information (NCEI) (noaa.gov)). <sentence_start/>The elevation data was directly obtained from the DEM, while the slope was calculated based on the DEM. <sentence_start/>The Topographic Wetness Index (TWI) was calculated using DEM<citation ref-type="bibr" rid="CR89" doi="10.1016/j.ecolind.2015.10.013" count="1"><sup>89</sup></citation>. <sentence_start/>Soil factors, including sand and silt, were obtained from the Harmonized World Soil Database version 2.0 (10.4060/cc3823en). <sentence_start/>The human footprint was from Last of the Wild, v2<citation ref-type="bibr" rid="CR90" doi="10.1038/s41597-022-01284-8" pmid="35440581" pmcid="PMC9018937" count="1"><sup>90</sup></citation>. <sentence_start/>To simulate the current susceptibility distribution of thermokarst lakes, climatic factors, including monthly maximum air temperature and precipitation, were obtained from WorldClim. <sentence_start/>The permafrost factor of active layer thickness (ALT) was sourced from a published dataset<citation ref-type="bibr" rid="CR91" count="1"><sup>91</sup></citation>.
Prediction of thermokarst lake

To predict future changes in thermokarst lake susceptibility under SSP1-2.6, SSP2-4.5, SSP3-7.0, and SSP5-8.5, we used monthly air temperature, precipitation ( ), and ALT<citation ref-type="bibr" rid="CR92" doi="10.1029/2023EF003573" count="1"><sup>92</sup></citation> data from five general circulation models (GCMs). <sentence_start/>We refined the resolution to 1 km using the delta approach. <sentence_start/>All data were masked to the study area and resampled to a spatial resolution of 0.0083° × 0.0083°. <sentence_start/>Our study used six machine learning models to assess the susceptibility of thermokarst lakes: Random Forest (RF), Generalized Additive Model (GAM), Generalized Boosted Regression Model (GBM), Classification and Regression Tree Analysis (CTA), Artificial Neural Network (ANN), and MaxEnt. <sentence_start/>We evaluated the performance of these models using Receiver Operating Characteristic (ROC) curves, Kappa statistics, and true skill statistics (TSS) (Supplementary Table 4). <sentence_start/>Based on these evaluations, we select the RF model, which performed best, for modeling. <sentence_start/>We set thresholds at 0.2, 0.4, 0.6, and 0.8 to classify susceptibility into five levels: very low, low, medium, high, and very high<citation ref-type="bibr" rid="CR93" doi="10.3390/rs13101974" count="1"><sup>93</sup></citation>. <sentence_start/>We identified the regions with moderate to very high levels as thermokarst lake affected areas. <sentence_start/>Then we estimated the lake area density (i.e., the area of lakes within a pixel) to calculate the future actual area of thermokarst lakes under different vegetation types. <sentence_start/>The standard error of the area density was used to quantify the uncertainty in these future projections (Supplementary Table 5).
Statistical analyses

In this study, we utilized one-way analysis of variance (ANOVA) with Tukey’s HSD post hoc comparisons to test differences in dissolved CH<sub>4</sub> concentrations and emission fluxes in thermokarst lakes among different vegetation types and during different periods at a significance level of <italic>P</italic> < 0.05. <sentence_start/>Regression analysis was employed to establish a linear relationship of dissolved CH<sub>4</sub> concentrations between the end of ice-covered and ice-melting period. <sentence_start/>This approach was used to interpolate concentration for lakes in our dataset lacking on-site sampling at the end of ice-melting period. <sentence_start/>These statistical analyses were performed using Python 3.11 (available at ). <sentence_start/>The regional estimates from Monte Carlo analysis were carried out using R v4.2.3 (available at ).
